### Question 1

Sometimes the same thing has two nicknames because it got named twice by people speaking different languages. The kidney has a Greek nickname (nephr/o) and a Latin nickname (ren/o). So 'nephritis' and 'renal failure' are both talking about the same bean-shaped organ, just wearing a different name tag.

### Question 2

Think of the bladder as a water balloon. The urethra is the ONE spout at the bottom that lets the water out of your body. The ureters are the TWO hoses up top that fill the balloon from the kidneys. Same first letters, but 'urethra' is the exit door and 'ureters' are the entrance hoses.

### Question 3

A suffix is the ending that tells you what KIND of word it is. '-uria' is a flag that says 'this is about pee.' So when you see 'hematuria,' you spot 'hemat' (blood) plus the pee flag, and you know it means blood showing up in the urine.

### Question 4

'Poly-' is like the word 'plenty' - it means a LOT. So polyuria is making a LOT of pee, way more than normal. Don't mix it up with 'oli-' (little, like oliguria) or 'an-' (none, like anuria). Poly = plenty of trips to the bathroom.

### Question 5

Same kidney root, two different endings. '-itis' means something is red and swollen and angry (inflammation) - nephritis. '-osis' just means something is 'off' or breaking down without the fire alarm of inflammation - nephrosis. The ending changes the whole story.

### Question 6

Picture a sink with the drain plugged. Water keeps coming in but can't get out, so it fills up and swells. 'Hydro' means water, 'nephr' means kidney - so hydronephrosis is a kidney that's ballooned up with backed-up pee because the drain is clogged.

### Question 7

The word 'cyst' really just means 'a squishy bag that holds liquid.' Your bladder IS a squishy bag that holds liquid (pee), so doctors use 'cyst/o' for the bladder. That's why cystitis means an irritated bladder. Careful though - 'cyt/o' with no 's' means cell, totally different.

### Question 8

'Py/o' means pus - the yellowish gunk your body makes when it's fighting germs. So pyuria means there's pus (germ-fighter cells) in the pee, which usually means there's an infection down there. Don't confuse it with 'poly-' (a lot) - py/o is about pus.

### Question 9

Break each big word into pieces. Cysto-scopy: bladder + look = peek inside the bladder with a tiny camera. Nephro-litho-tomy: kidney + stone + cut = make a cut to take out a kidney stone. The endings tell you the ACTION: '-scopy' is looking, '-tomy' is cutting.

### Question 10

'Dys-' is the 'ugh, this is bad or hard' prefix (like 'dysfunction'). Add the pee flag '-uria' and you get dysuria: peeing that hurts or is hard to do. So burning when you go to the bathroom is dysuria.

### Question 11

Same kidney word, one ending swapped, totally different surgery. '-ectomy' = take it OUT (like 'exit'). '-stomy' = make a new MOUTH or opening (a 'stoma') so stuff can drain. So nephrectomy removes the kidney; nephrostomy just makes a drainage hole into it, which is often only kept for a while until the blockage is fixed.

### Question 12

Think of the bladder as a balloon with a drawstring (the sphincter). Retention is when you CAN'T let the pee out even though you need to. Incontinence is when pee leaks out when you don't want it to - sometimes because the drawstring won't stay closed, and sometimes because the balloon squeezes on its own. One is mostly a 'stuck holding' problem, the other a 'can't hold' problem.
